key_terms.meaning: grad φ = ∇φ = (∂φ/∂x)i + (∂φ/∂y)j + (∂φ/∂z)k; a vector pointing in the direction of fastest increase of the scalar field φ, with length equal to that fastest rate
dφ/ds along a unit direction â equals ∇φ · â; the rate of change of φ per unit distance in that direction
A vector â with |â| = 1, written â = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k with a₁² + a₂² + a₃² = 1; only unit vectors may be used in a directional derivative
∇ = i ∂/∂x + j ∂/∂y + k ∂/∂z; a differential operator that becomes gradient, divergence or curl depending on what it acts on
div F = ∇ · F = ∂F₁/∂x + ∂F₂/∂y + ∂F₃/∂z; a scalar measuring the net outflow per unit volume at a point
curl F = ∇ × F, the formal cross product of ∇ with F; a vector measuring the local rotation or spin of the field
A vector field F with ∇ · F = 0 everywhere; its flux through any closed surface is zero
A vector field F with ∇ × F = 0 everywhere; its line integral between two points is path independent
A scalar function φ with F = ∇φ; it exists for an irrotational field in a simply connected region and is found by integrating the components of F and matching constants
∫_C F · dr = ∫_C (F₁dx + F₂dy + F₃dz) along a curve C; adds the tangential component of F along the curve
For a force field F moving a particle along C, work W = ∫_C F · dr, measured in joules when F is in newtons and dr in metres
A field that is the gradient of a scalar potential; equivalently ∇ × F = 0, and its line integral depends only on the endpoints
∬_S F · n̂ dS over a surface S with unit normal n̂; adds the normal component of F over the sheet
The surface integral ∬_S F · n̂ dS; the amount of F crossing S per unit time when F is a velocity field
∭_V f dV over a solid V, evaluated as a repeated ordinary integral in a suitable coordinate system
For a plane region R with boundary C taken anticlockwise, ∮_C (M dx + N dy) = ∬_R (∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y) dx dy
∮_C F · dr = ∬_S (∇ × F) · n̂ dS, where C is the boundary of the open surface S with compatible orientation
∬_S F · n̂ dS = ∭_V (∇ · F) dV, where S is the closed surface bounding the volume V and n̂ points outward
κ = |dT̂/ds|, the rate at which the unit tangent T̂ turns with arc length s; κ = 1/ρ where ρ is the radius of curvature
τ = −(dB̂/ds) · N̂, the rate at which the curve twists out of its osculating plane; zero for a plane curve

takeaways: The gradient turns a scalar field into a vector; the directional derivative is just that vector dotted with a unit direction, so the maximum rate of increase is |∇φ|.
All three first-order operators come from the same ∇, so their product rules and the identities ∇ × ∇φ = 0 and ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0 follow from ordinary differentiation.
Zero divergence means no sources (solenoidal); zero curl means no rotation (irrotational) and guarantees a scalar potential.
A line integral of a force field is work, and for an irrotational field the path does not matter — only the two endpoints do.
Surface and volume integrals are not new calculus; write the surface or solid in parameters, put in the Jacobian factor, and integrate.
Green, Stokes and Gauss are one idea in three settings: an integral over a boundary equals an integral of a derivative over the inside.
Green's theorem is Stokes' theorem restricted to a flat region in the xy-plane.
For space curves, curvature measures bending and torsion measures twisting; both come from derivatives of the position vector with respect to arc length.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always demand a full verification of one of the three integral theorems on a stated region, or the construction of a scalar potential — so the marks sit in correct limits, correct normals and correct orientation, not in the statement.

bank.q: Define the gradient of a scalar field and the directional derivative in a given direction. Show that the directional derivative equals ∇φ · â for a unit vector â, and state the direction in which it is largest and smallest.
outline: Define ∇φ in Cartesian coordinates
Show dφ/ds = ∇φ · â using the chain rule
Maximum along ∇φ, value |∇φ|; minimum along −∇φ
Zero along directions perpendicular to ∇φ

bank.q: Explain the three ways the operator ∇ acts, give the Cartesian formula for each, and prove that ∇ × (∇φ) = 0 and ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.
outline: Gradient on a scalar gives a vector; divergence on a vector gives a scalar; curl on a vector gives a vector
Write the three formulas component by component
Expand the mixed second derivatives and cancel using equality of mixed partials
State the converse: curl-free implies a potential in a simply connected region

bank.q: Define a solenoidal field and an irrotational field. Give one physical situation for each and state the condition each satisfies in terms of divergence and curl.
outline: Solenoidal: ∇ · F = 0
Irrotational: ∇ × F = 0
Example: incompressible flow for solenoidal; electrostatic or gravitational field for irrotational
Note that a field can be both, and then it satisfies Laplace's equation

bank.q: State Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem and Gauss divergence theorem. For each, say what kind of integral is converted into what kind, and what condition the boundary or surface must satisfy.
outline: Green: closed plane curve to double integral over the enclosed region, anticlockwise orientation
Stokes: closed curve to open surface it bounds, orientation by right-hand rule
Gauss: closed surface to enclosed volume, outward normal
Dimensions of the objects in each theorem: 1D boundary, 2D surface, 3D volume

bank.q: Find the directional derivative of φ = x²y + yz³ at the point (1, −1, 2) in the direction of the vector i + 2j + 2k, and find the maximum rate of increase of φ at that point.
outline: Compute ∇φ = 2xy i + (x² + z³) j + 3yz² k
Evaluate at the point
Normalise the direction vector by dividing by its length 3
Directional derivative = ∇φ · â; maximum rate = |∇φ|

bank.q: Show that F = (y + z)i + (z + x)j + (x + y)k is irrotational and find a scalar potential φ with F = ∇φ.
outline: Compute curl F and show all three components vanish
Integrate ∂φ/∂x = y + z with respect to x
Match the other two components to fix the arbitrary function of y and z
Verify by taking the gradient of the answer

bank.q: Find the work done by the force F = (x² − y²)i + 2xy j in moving a particle along the parabola y = x² from (0, 0) to (1, 1).
outline: Parameterise the path with x = t, y = t², or express y in terms of x
Write dr = dx i + dy j and substitute
Reduce to a single integral in one variable
State the answer with units if force is in newtons and distance in metres

bank.q: Verify Green's theorem for ∮_C (3x² − 8y²) dx + (4y − 6xy) dy, where C is the boundary of the region bounded by x = 0, y = 0 and x + y = 1.
outline: Identify M and N, compute ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y
Do the double integral over the triangle with proper limits
Do the line integral in three pieces along the three edges, with correct direction
Show both values agree

bank.q: Verify Stokes' theorem for F = (x² − y²)i + 2xy j over the rectangle in the xy-plane bounded by x = 0, x = a, y = 0, y = b.
outline: Compute ∇ × F, which here points along k
Flux of the curl through the flat rectangle equals (curl F)₃ times the area
Do the line integral round the four edges in anticlockwise order
Compare the two results

bank.q: Verify the Gauss divergence theorem for F = 4xz i − y² j + yz k over the cube bounded by x = 0, x = 1, y = 0, y = 1, z = 0, z = 1.
outline: Compute ∇ · F and integrate over the unit cube
Compute the flux through all six faces, taking the outward normal on each
Faces with zero contribution can be noted and skipped
Show the two values are equal

bank.q: For the helix r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + ct k, find the unit tangent, the unit normal, the curvature and the torsion.
outline: Compute r′(t) and the arc length element |r′(t)|
T̂ = r′/|r′|; then dT̂/ds = (dT̂/dt)/(ds/dt)
κ = |dT̂/ds|, giving a/(a² + c²)
Use τ = −(dB̂/ds) · N̂ or the triple-product formula to get c/(a² + c²)

bank.q: Show that the line integral of an irrotational field between two fixed points is independent of the path. Use this to compute the work done by such a field along two different paths joining the same two points and compare the answers.
outline: Write F = ∇φ and use dφ = ∇φ · dr
Integral equals φ(B) − φ(A), depending only on endpoints
Choose two explicit paths and evaluate
Comment on what fails if the region has a hole, such as F = (−y i + x j)/(x² + y²)

bank.q: Use the divergence theorem to evaluate a surface integral of your choice over a closed surface by converting it to a volume integral. Explain why the surface must be closed and why the normal must point outward, and what changes if the surface is open.
outline: State the theorem with the closed-surface and outward-normal conditions
Choose F whose divergence is simple and set up the triple integral with correct limits
Compute and compare with the direct surface calculation for one face as a check
For an open surface the theorem fails; close it with a cap or use Stokes instead

bank.q: Obtain Green's theorem as the plane case of Stokes' theorem, and use it to express the area of a plane region as a line integral round its boundary.
outline: Take F = M i + N j with no z dependence and a flat surface in the xy-plane
Reduce the surface integral of the curl to a double integral of ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y
Choose M = −y/2, N = x/2 to get area = ½∮(x dy − y dx)
Apply to one region, for example an ellipse, as a check

glossary.def: A function that assigns one number to each point of space, such as temperature or pressure.
A function that assigns a vector to each point of space, such as fluid velocity or electric field.
The set of points where a scalar field equals a constant; the gradient is normal to it.
The symbolic vector ∇ = i∂/∂x + j∂/∂y + k∂/∂z used to define gradient, divergence and curl.
∇φ, the vector of partial derivatives of a scalar field, normal to the level surfaces.
The rate of change of a scalar field per unit distance along a chosen unit direction.
∇ · F, a scalar giving the net outflow of a vector field per unit volume at a point.
∇ × F, a vector giving the local rotation of a vector field.
∇²φ = ∇ · (∇φ) = ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂y² + ∂²φ/∂z².
Having zero divergence everywhere, so that no sources or sinks exist inside the region.
Having zero curl everywhere, so that the field has no local spin.
A scalar φ with F = ∇φ; it exists when F is irrotational on a simply connected region.
An integral of a field along a curve, written ∫_C F · dr.
The line integral of a vector field round a closed curve, ∮_C F · dr.
A field whose line integral between two points does not depend on the path taken.
An integral of a field over a surface, written ∬_S F · n̂ dS for the flux form.
The total amount of a vector field passing through a surface, counting only the normal component.
An integral of a function over a solid region, written ∭_V f dV.
The choice of direction of the normal to a surface, or of travel along a curve, fixed by convention.
A curve that starts and ends at the same point and does not cross itself in between.
The distance measured along a curve, s = ∫|r′(t)| dt.
T̂ = dr/ds, the direction of travel along a curve in terms of arc length.
N̂ = (dT̂/ds)/|dT̂/ds|, the direction in which the curve is turning.
The plane at a point of a space curve that contains both the tangent and the principal normal.
κ = |dT̂/ds|, measuring how quickly the curve bends; its reciprocal is the radius of curvature.
τ, measuring how quickly a space curve twists out of its osculating plane; zero for plane curves.
